title_en: Prefaces to the Books of Samuel and Kings, the Books of Solomon, and Daniel
author: Jerome
addressee: Christian readers generally; in the Daniel preface, Paula and Eustochium
occasion: Jerome defends and introduces his new Latin translations of the Hebrew Scriptures, explaining the Hebrew canon, his method, and why he excludes or marks certain additions found in Greek versions.
argument: Jerome argues that the Old Testament canon consists of twenty-two Hebrew books, matching the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and that anything outside these is apocryphal. He defends his practice of translating from the Hebrew rather than the Greek Septuagint, insisting that he has not altered the Hebrew truth. In the preface to the Solomonic books he distinguishes canonical books from edifying but non-canonical writings such as Wisdom and Sirach. In the Daniel preface he states that the churches of the Lord Savior do not read Daniel according to the Septuagint interpreters, but use Theodotion's edition, and he expresses ignorance about why this happened. He also notes that the stories of Susanna, the hymn of the three youths, and Bel and the Dragon are not in the Hebrew Daniel, and that he has prefixed a mark and subjoined them as if killing them.

outline.move: Jerome explains the twenty-two-letter Hebrew alphabet as the basis for the twenty-two-book Hebrew canon, lists the books in their Hebrew order, excludes apocryphal writings, and defends his translation from the Hebrew.

Jerome dedicates his translation of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs to his patrons, distinguishes these canonical Solomonic books from Wisdom and Sirach, and defends his fresh translation from the Hebrew.

Jerome notes that the churches use Theodotion's Daniel rather than the Septuagint, explains that Daniel is written partly in Aramaic, discusses the non-Hebrew additions of Susanna, the three youths' hymn, and Bel and the Dragon, and asks Paula and Eustochium for their prayers.

scripture: Jerome uses the Hebrew names and order of the biblical books, with the Hebrew canon divided into Law, Prophets, and Writings. Psalms are numbered according to the Hebrew text, which Jerome follows; in the preface he cites Psalm 38 (Hebrew numbering), which corresponds to Psalm 39 in the Septuagint and Vulgate numbering. Citations should be given in modern form with Hebrew Psalm numbering, e.g. Psalm 38 (Hebrew) = Psalm 39 (LXX/Vulgate).
uncertain: The exact date of each preface; the range c. 390–393 is approximate.
The identity of the 'quendam de præceptoribus Judæorum' quoted in the Daniel preface.
Whether the 'quidam e nostris' in the Daniel preface refers to a specific known person.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He also notes that the stories of Susanna, the hymn of the three youths, and Bel and the Dragon are not in the Hebrew Daniel, and that he has prefixed a mark and subjoined them as if killing them.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: quas nos, quia in tote orbe dispersæ sunt, veru anteposito, easque jugulante subjecimus
_unresolved_facts.fix: Jerome notes these stories are not in the Hebrew Daniel, and that he has prefixed a mark (veru anteposito) and subjoined them as if killing them (easque jugulante subjecimus) because they are dispersed throughout the whole world (in tote orbe dispersæ sunt)—i.e., to avoid appearing to have mutilated the book for the uninformed, not because he accepts them as authentic.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Origen, source_forms: ['Origenes'], who: An earlier Christian scholar to whom Africanus opposed an argument about Susanna.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: illud opponere quod Origeni quoque Africanus opposuit
_unresolved_facts.fix: Africanus, source_forms: ['Africanus'], who: Julius Africanus, a Christian writer who opposed Origen on the question of Susanna. Origen is not a named character in the text; he is mentioned only as the one whom Africanus opposed.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul the Apostle, how_marked: Quoted directly with citation to 2 Corinthians 12, sections: [daniel]
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Denique et Apostolum nostrum, videlicet ut eruditum virum, et qui legem ab Hebræis didicisset, non fuisse ausum affirmare se raptum in corpore, sed dixisse: 'Sive in corpore sive extra corpus : Nescio, Deus scit' [2. Cor. 12.]
_unresolved_facts.fix: Paul the Apostle, how_marked: Introduced indirectly ('Denique et Apostolum nostrum...') with a paraphrased rather than directly quoted statement, then a brief formulaic quotation with citation to 2 Corinthians 12, sections: [daniel]

_unresolved_facts.claim: A Hebrew teacher or Jewish instructor, how_marked: Introduced by Jerome as 'quendam de præceptoribus Judæorum' and his speech reported indirectly, sections: [daniel]
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Audivi ego quendam de præceptoribus Judæorum, cum Susannæ derideret historiam... His et talibus argumentis apocryphas in libro Ecclesiæ fabulas arguebat
_unresolved_facts.fix: A Hebrew teacher or Jewish instructor, how_marked: Introduced by Jerome as 'quendam de præceptoribus Judæorum' with extensive indirect discourse including multiple arguments and rhetorical questions, sections: [daniel]

_unresolved_facts.claim: Jesu filius Nave: Joshua son of Nun
_unresolved_facts.fix: Jesu filio Nave: Joshua son of Nun (the source has filio, not filius)

_unresolved_facts.claim: Josue ben Nun: Joshua son of Nun
_unresolved_facts.fix: Josue ben Nun: Joshua son of Nun (the source has Jehosue/Josue ben Nun with Hebrew יהוסע בן נון)

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Fertur et Panæretos Iesu filii Sirach liber, et alius pseudepigraphus, qui Sapientia Salomonis inscribitur
_unresolved_facts.fix: Panæretos: All-Virtue (a Greek title meaning 'comprising all virtue'); the name refers to the book's title, not to Sirach as a name. The book is 'Iesu filii Sirach' (Jesus son of Sirach).

_unresolved_facts.claim: In the preface to the Solomonic books he distinguishes these canonical Solomonic books from Wisdom and Sirach
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Quorum priorem Hebraicum reperi : non Ecclesiasticum, ut apud Latinos, sed Parabolas prænotatum, cui juncti erant Ecclesiastes et Canticum canticorum : ut similitudinem Salomonis, non solum librorum numero, sed etiam materiarum genere coæquaret
_unresolved_facts.fix: In the preface to the Solomonic books he distinguishes these canonical Solomonic books from Wisdom and Sirach, and notes that Sirach (which he found in Hebrew) was titled 'Parabolas' not 'Ecclesiasticus,' and was bound together with Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs to match Solomon's likeness in number and kind of material.
